442.title: Many doors to one God
442.hook: a man who hated Krishna merges into him, and Narada explains how
442.carry: one God, through the form you love
442.tomorrow: the universe in a toddler's mouth
442.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep several deities on one shrine, while each person may hold one as their ishta devata, the chosen form of God they love most; teachers often cite Yoga Sutra 1.39 for meditating on the form that is dear to you.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: or, the breath. A long breath out, a small rest at the bottom. Today Patanjali keeps opening doors, and an old story shows how many.
screen: `OR THE BREATH — A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira's great royal ceremony is underway when a king named Shishupala stands up and insults Krishna, again and again, in front of everyone. In the Mahabharata, Krishna had promised Shishupala's mother he would forgive a hundred offenses. When the count runs out, Shishupala falls. And then something stuns the hall: a light rises from the fallen man and enters Krishna. Yudhishthira can't make sense of it. A man who hated the Lord, merged into him? Later, in the Bhagavata, he asks the sage Narada how.
screen: `SHISHUPALA INSULTS KRISHNA.` → `A LIGHT ENTERS KRISHNA.` → `HOW?`

segments.voice: Narada's answer is one of the boldest passages in the tradition. What matters, he says, is a mind fixed wholly on the Lord. The cowherd women of Vraja reached Krishna through longing. King Kamsa through fear: he thought of nothing else. Shishupala and other kings through hatred. Krishna's own clan through kinship. The Pandavas through affection. Sages like Narada through devotion. So, he concludes, fix the mind on Krishna by any means. Devotees hear the obvious next step: then why not by love? Patanjali makes a quieter version of the same point. Sutras 1.35 to 1.39 each carry the little word or. Or a fine sense experience that holds the mind steady. Or the sorrowless, luminous one, which the commentator Vyasa places in the heart. Or a mind resting on someone free of attachment, a saint or a great teacher. Or what's known in dream and deep sleep. And 1.39, wide open: or by meditating on whatever you find dear. Vyasa says that isn't a loophole: once the mind steadies on what it loves, it can steady anywhere. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath both. Hindus speak of an ishta devata, a chosen deity: one God, met through the form a person loves most. That's why one home shrine has Krishna in the center and another has Shiva or the Goddess, and why one grandmother prays to Ganesha first and to Krishna longest. Some modern teachers link 1.39 to this. Not gods competing. One house, and each person comes in by the door they love.
screen: `LONGING, FEAR, EVEN HATRED.` · `WHY NOT BY LOVE?` · `1.39: WHATEVER YOU FIND DEAR.` · then, large: `ISHTA DEVATA: THE FORM YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: Today you choose the door. If you pray, your ishta devata, the form of God dear to you: Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess, Ganesha. If you don't, a soft light in the chest, the face of someone whose goodness you trust, or an image you love like the sea or a flame. Rest your attention there. When the mind wanders, come back through the same door.
Or. Five more times in sutras 1.35 to 1.39: a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, and whatever you find dear.
screen: `OR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one God, through the form you love. Many doors, one house. Until tomorrow.

443.title: The universe in Krishna's mouth
443.hook: little Krishna is caught eating dirt, and his mother looks in his mouth
443.carry: smaller than small, greater than great
443.tomorrow: an archer who sees only the bird
443.howItsDone: Yashoda's vision is a favorite of Krishna's childhood stories, often retold around Janmashtami, and Hindus bow to small murtis and shaligram stones as the Lord of all; students of the Yoga Sutras treat 1.40 as the sign that the mind has been steadied.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: one God, through the form you love. Many doors, one house. Today, what a steadied mind can hold, and a mother who saw it.
screen: `ONE GOD, THROUGH THE FORM YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: In the village of Gokula, little Krishna's friends run to his mother, Yashoda: he's been eating dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, eyes wide, and says they're lying. If you don't believe me, look in my mouth. So she says: open. He opens his mouth. And inside, the Bhagavata says, Yashoda sees the whole universe: the sky and the directions, mountains, islands and oceans, wind and fire, the moon and the stars, and her own village, with herself standing in it.
screen: `HE'S BEEN EATING DIRT.` → `OPEN YOUR MOUTH.` → `THE WHOLE UNIVERSE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: She's frightened, then amazed. Then, the story says, Krishna covers the vision with a mother's love, and she lifts him onto her lap as if nothing happened. A toddler you could carry on one hip, holding everything. Hindu scripture has a phrase for this: smaller than the small, greater than the great. The Katha Upanishad says it, and so does the Shvetashvatara, which you met a couple of weeks ago: the divine self, hidden in every heart, is both. It's why a Hindu can bow to a thumb-sized murti, or a smooth black shaligram stone, and mean the Lord of the whole universe. Size was never the measure. Now Patanjali. Sutra 1.40, in paraphrase: the yogi's mastery reaches from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude. Paramanu, the smallest atom. Parama mahat, the greatest greatness. Vashikara, mastery. The commentator Vyasa explains: a mind steadied through any of yesterday's doors can rest on the subtlest object without slipping, and on the vastest without scattering. Small doesn't make it fidget. Huge doesn't make it lose its grip. Many teachers read the two together: the divine is smaller than small and greater than great, and a practiced mind becomes able to hold both. The little murti on the shelf and the night sky over the roof aren't two different subjects. The sutra is also a hinge. The list of doors is done, and next comes what happens inside absorption itself, with a mind like a clear crystal.
screen: `A TODDLER HOLDING EVERYTHING.` · `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.` · `1.40: PARAMANU TO PARAMA MAHAT.` · then, large: `A MIND THAT HOLDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on the smallest thing you can feel, a fingertip on your knee, then widen to the whole body, the room, the sky over the roof, and come back to the fingertip. If you pray, picture the form of God you love, small enough to sit in your palm, then as wide as the sky. Notice whether the steadiness holds as the size changes.
Vashikara, mastery, having it under control. Sutra 1.40: a steadied mind can rest on anything, from the tiniest particle to the greatest expanse, the way Yashoda found the universe in a toddler.
screen: `VASHIKARA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: smaller than small, greater than great. A toddler's mouth, and the whole universe inside. Day four hundred forty-three, done.

444.title: Arjuna and the bird
444.hook: Drona tests his students on a wooden bird, and only Arjuna sees nothing else
444.carry: the clear mind takes the color of its object
444.tomorrow: the sage who knew only the words
444.howItsDone: Hindus go for darshan, standing before the deity in a temple or at a home shrine to see and be seen; teachers of classical yoga describe samapatti as the mind becoming transparent to its object, and guide students from coarse objects, like an image or a flame, toward subtler ones.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: smaller than small, greater than great, and a mind steady on either. Today, an archer who saw only one thing.
screen: `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.`

segments.voice: The teacher Drona has a wooden bird set high in a tree and lines up his young students, the princes, with their bows. Before anyone shoots, he asks each one a question. Do you see the bird? The tree? Me? Your brothers? Yudhishthira, the eldest, says yes: the tree, you, my brothers, the bird. Drona sends him aside without letting him shoot. One by one, the others say the same and step aside. Then Arjuna steps up.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `EVERYTHING, SAY THE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: What do you see? Only the bird, Arjuna says. Not the tree, not you. Describe the bird. I see its head, not its body. Shoot, says Drona, and the arrow takes the head clean off. Popular retellings make it the bird's eye; in the Mahabharata it's the head. Either way, Arjuna's mind had taken the shape of one thing. Patanjali describes that from the inside. Sutra 1.41, in paraphrase: when the turnings of the mind have dwindled, it becomes like a fine, transparent jewel and takes on the form of whatever it rests on. Set a clear crystal on red cloth and it shows red; on blue silk, blue. That coinciding is samapatti. Then he maps the stages. Savitarka: absorption on a coarse object, still mixed with the word, the thing and the idea. The commentator Vyasa's example is a cow: the sound cow, the animal, and the thought of a cow, tangled together. Nirvitarka: memory cleaned out, and only the object shines. Sutra 1.44 says the same two steps happen with subtle objects, and 1.46 calls all of these samadhi with seed, absorption still resting on something. Here's the Hindu practice it lights up. If the mind takes the color of what it rests on, then what you rest it on matters. Many teachers read darshan this way: before the deity in a temple or at the home shrine, Hindus stand and simply look, and are looked at, letting the mind take that color. Not analyzing the murti. Seeing it, the way Arjuna saw the bird.
screen: `ONLY THE BIRD. ONLY ITS HEAD.` · `1.41: THE MIND LIKE CLEAR CRYSTAL.` · `WORD, THING, IDEA; THEN ONLY THE THING.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: SEEING, AND BEING SEEN.`

segments.voice: Light a lamp or a candle if you can, or look at an image of God you love, or any object near you. Notice the name arrive, then the ideas: brass, old, needs polishing. Let them go and just look: shape, light, color. Then close your eyes and hold it without words, like the crystal on the cloth.
Samapatti, coinciding, the mind taking the form of what it rests on. The stages move from thought to without, on coarse objects and on subtle ones, the steps of samadhi with seed.

segments.voice: Your line: the clear mind takes the color of its object. So choose what you rest it on. See you tomorrow.

445.title: The sage who knew only the words
445.hook: Narada has studied everything, and admits he knows only the words
445.carry: ritambhara: knowing it, not knowing about it
445.howItsDone: Hindu teachers honor scripture study but often say it must ripen into direct knowing; in classical yoga, ritambhara prajna is described as the fruit of mature absorption, set apart from book learning and reasoning, both valued as steps on the way.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the clear mind takes the color of its object, like Arjuna seeing only the bird. Today, what the clearest mind knows.
screen: `THE CLEAR MIND TAKES THE COLOR.`

segments.voice: Narada is the sage who has studied everything. In the Chandogya Upanishad he comes to another sage, Sanatkumara, and asks to be taught. Sanatkumara says: first tell me what you already know. So Narada lists it. The four Vedas. The old histories and stories. Grammar, mathematics, logic, the rites for the ancestors, the lore of the stars and of the gods, the fine arts. It's a long list. Then he says the line the whole chapter hangs on.
screen: `TEACH ME, SIR.` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW.` → `A VERY LONG LIST.`

segments.voice: Sir, I know only the words. I don't know the self. I've heard from people like you that whoever knows the self crosses beyond sorrow, and I am in sorrow. Take me across. Sanatkumara's reply is gentle and blunt: all you've studied is only name. Then he leads him, step by step, toward what the Upanishad calls fullness. That's a real Hindu teaching, and it runs deep: knowing about the sacred isn't the same as knowing it. Narada's learning isn't mocked. It's the start, not the end. Patanjali gives that difference a name. Sutra 1.47: when the subtle absorption without reflection becomes fully clear, there's inner serenity, adhyatma prasada. Sutra 1.48: there, wisdom is ritambhara, truth-bearing. Ritam echoes rita, the old Vedic word for the cosmic order, the rightness that turns the seasons, tied to truth itself. So ritambhara is wisdom that carries the truth in it, because the mind adds no color of its own. Sutra 1.49 says how it differs. What you learn from testimony, a teacher or a book, and from inference, reasoning it out, is about things in general. Truth-bearing wisdom knows the particular, as it is. Narada knew all the words, and not the self. Then sutra 1.50: every experience leaves an impression, a samskara, a groove in the mind. This wisdom leaves a groove so deep it blocks the old ruts. One groove is left, its own. Tomorrow, what happens when even that goes quiet.
screen: `I KNOW ONLY THE WORDS.` · `KNOWING ABOUT ISN'T KNOWING.` · `1.48: RITAMBHARA, TRUTH-BEARING.` · then, large: `A GROOVE THAT BLOCKS THE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes a small bell rings at puja. Ring one if you have it, or tap a glass, or listen to whatever sound is near. Notice the word bell arrive, and the ideas about it. Let them go and stay with the sound itself, this sound, as it fades. When it's gone, rest in the quiet it leaves, then begin again.
Truth-bearing wisdom. Ritambhara prajna, sutra 1.48: the knowing that arises in the clearest absorption, full of truth, and aimed at the particular, as it is.
screen: `TRUTH-BEARING WISDOM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ritambhara, knowing it, not knowing about it. Narada's whole library, and still: take me across. That's day four hundred forty-five.

segments.voice: Bengal, the 1860s, the Kali temple at Dakshineswar near Kolkata. Its priest, Ramakrishna, loves the Goddess Kali the way a child loves his mother. A wandering monk named Totapuri arrives, a teacher of the path of knowledge, and tells him: go beyond all forms. Ramakrishna sits to meditate, and every time, the radiant form of the Mother rises before him. He can't get past her.
screen: `THE PRIEST WHO LOVES KALI.` → `GO BEYOND ALL FORMS.` → `THE MOTHER RISES, EVERY TIME.`

segments.voice: In his own telling, as his followers recorded it, Totapuri grows stern, picks up a sliver of glass, and presses its point between Ramakrishna's eyebrows. Fix your mind here. Ramakrishna sits again. When the Mother's form appears, he takes knowledge like a sword and cuts through it, and the last barrier falls away. His followers say he stayed absorbed for three days. That's the territory of sutra 1.51. Tasyapi nirodhe sarva nirodhan nirbijah samadhih. When even that is stilled, everything stilled, there is seedless absorption. Even that: the impression left by yesterday's truth-bearing wisdom, the last good groove. When it too goes quiet, nothing is left that could sprout. Nirbija, without seed. The commentator Vyasa says the seer then rests alone, pure and free, which loops back to sutra 1.3: the seer rests in its own form. Chapter one began with the definition of yoga and ends with yoga complete. Now the Hindu teaching, held in two hands. Many teachers say God is both with form, saguna, and beyond all form, nirguna. Vedanta calls the deepest absorption nirvikalpa, without distinctions, a close cousin of Patanjali's seedless state. And then the part people love: Ramakrishna came back, and went on loving Kali all his life. For him, the formless and the Mother were one, the way fire and its power to burn are one. Devotional schools weigh it differently and treasure the form itself; that's a real conversation inside Hinduism. Tomorrow, chapter two begins.
screen: `GLASS BETWEEN THE EYEBROWS.` · `1.51: EVEN THAT IS STILLED.` · `WITH FORM, AND BEYOND FORM.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK, STILL LOVING KALI.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture the form of God you love, or a lamp's flame, and rest with it for a while. Then, without pushing it away, let the picture soften and fade, and sit holding nothing in particular, just aware. If a thought comes, let it go without picking up a new support. It's only a taste of letting go of even the good seed.
Seedless. Nirbija samadhi, sutra 1.51: when even the last good impression is stilled, nothing remains that could sprout, and the seer rests in itself.
screen: `SEEDLESS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seedless, even the holiest seed is let go. And Ramakrishna still came home to his Mother. Chapter one, done.

447.title: Parvati's tapas
447.hook: a princess does fierce tapas for Shiva, and a stranger tries to talk her out of it
447.carry: tapas, study, surrender: the yoga of action
447.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vows such as Monday fasts for Shiva, and in many regions women keep Hartalika Teej in memory of Parvati's tapas; some who follow the Yoga Sutras practice kriya yoga as a daily rhythm of a kept discipline, scripture or mantra, and offering the day's actions to God.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: seedless, even the holiest seed let go, and Ramakrishna still came home to his Mother. Today chapter two begins, with a princess on a mountain.
screen: `SEEDLESS — EVEN THE HOLIEST SEED.`

segments.voice: Parvati, daughter of the Himalaya, has set her heart on Shiva, the great ascetic, and Shiva doesn't notice. So she goes up into the mountains and does tapas. In Kalidasa's poem and in the Puranas she sits between fires in the summer heat and in icy water in winter, and eats only leaves that fall by themselves, then not even those. One day a young holy man arrives, polite and curious. Why, he asks, would someone like you burn herself away for Shiva? Ash on his body, snakes for jewelry, a cremation ground for a home.
screen: `SHE SETS HER HEART ON SHIVA.` → `FIRE IN SUMMER, ICE IN WINTER.` → `WHY HIM, OF ALL PEOPLE?`

segments.voice: Parvati defends Shiva and gets up to leave. The stranger stops her and shows his true form: Shiva himself, saying her tapas has won him. That's why she's called Aparna, the one who gave up even leaves, and why women in many regions keep Hartalika Teej, a fast that remembers her tapas, and many Hindus keep Monday fasts for Shiva. Tapas, literally heat, is one of the oldest words in Hinduism, and Patanjali puts it first in sutra 2.1, which opens chapter two: tapah svadhyaya ishvara pranidhanani kriya yogah. Discipline, study and surrender to the Lord are the yoga of action. Kriya means action: yoga you do in daily life. The commentator Vyasa says chapter one spoke to a settled mind, and chapter two to a scattered one. Tapas is the heat of keeping a vow when comfort pulls the other way, and here Vyasa gentles Parvati's extremes: practice it only so far as it doesn't disturb a calm, clear mind. A later commentator adds: or the body's balance. The Gita even counts truthful, kind speech as tapas. Svadhyaya, one's own study: the sacred texts, and, Vyasa adds, repeating om or a mantra. Ishvara pranidhana: offering every action to the Lord and letting go of its fruits, like the Gita's line, whatever you do, eat or give, offer it to me. Sutra 2.2 says why: to cultivate absorption and to thin the afflictions. Thin, the way water wears down stone. Parvati had all three: the heat, the steady remembering of Shiva, and a heart already given.
screen: `HER TAPAS WINS SHIVA.` · `2.1: TAPAS, STUDY, SURRENDER.` · `HEAT THAT DOESN'T HARM.` · then, large: `THINNING THE AFFLICTIONS.`

segments.voice: Try all three in miniature. Tapas: sit still for a few breaths, even when the body wants to shift. Svadhyaya: say one line you love slowly, Om, a mantra or a verse, and really hear it. Surrender: offer this sit to God if you pray, or simply let go of needing it to be good. Then rest on the breath.
Kriya yoga. The yoga of action in sutra 2.1: discipline, study and surrender to the Lord, practiced to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions.
screen: `KRIYA YOGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: tapas, study, surrender, the yoga of action. Parvati's heat, kept gently. Until tomorrow.

448.title: The Yaksha's question
448.hook: a voice at a lake asks Yudhishthira what the greatest wonder is
448.carry: five afflictions, one root: seeing wrongly
448.tomorrow: ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent
448.howItsDone: Hindus retell the yaksha's questions as a test of wisdom, and students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five kleshas as the root diagnosis of suffering; some teachers ask them to trace everyday reactions back to these roots in meditation and daily life.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: kriya yoga, tapas, study and surrender, practiced to thin the afflictions. Today, what exactly gets thinned, and a riddle at a lake.
screen: `TAPAS, STUDY, SURRENDER.`

segments.voice: The five Pandava brothers are deep in the forest, exhausted and thirsty. Nakula finds a clear lake, and a voice calls out: answer my questions first, then drink. He drinks anyway, and falls. Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima come looking, ignore the voice, and fall by the water too. Then Yudhishthira arrives, sees his brothers lying there, and does what none of them did. He listens. The voice is a yaksha, a spirit of the lake, and it asks question after question.
screen: `ANSWER FIRST, THEN DRINK.` → `FOUR BROTHERS FALL.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA LISTENS.`

segments.voice: One of them: what is the greatest wonder? Yudhishthira answers: every day, creatures go to the house of death, and those who remain want to live forever. What could be more wonderful than that? The yaksha turns out to be Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's divine father, and gives the brothers back their lives. Hold that answer up to Patanjali. Sutra 2.3: avidya asmita raga dvesha abhiniveshah kleshah. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life are the afflictions. Klesha means affliction, a cause of pain. Abhinivesha, clinging to life, is last on the list, and sutra 2.9 says it's found even in the wise. That's the yaksha's wonder: everyone sees death, and lives as if it won't come for them. Under it are the others. Raga, the pull toward what pleased. Dvesha, the push away from what hurt. Asmita, the sense of a separate me who is pleased and hurt. And first, avidya, ignorance: not a lack of facts, but seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts. The next sutra calls ignorance the field the other four grow in. Here's the teaching, plainly. For Patanjali the deepest root of human trouble isn't bad luck, and even misdeeds grow from something underneath. It's a mistake about what's real, which the mind then defends. So the cure is seeing clearly, not only trying harder. This week walked toward it: many doors, a toddler's mouth, the archer's bird, Narada's words, Ramakrishna's last seed, Parvati's heat, and now the roots.
screen: `THE GREATEST WONDER.` · `2.3: FIVE AFFLICTIONS.` · `PULL, PUSH, I-NESS, AND THE ROOT.` · then, large: `ONE ROOT: SEEING WRONGLY.`

segments.voice: As thoughts come, sort them gently into the five: wanting something is attraction, avoiding something is aversion, me and my image is I-ness, a flicker of fear about the future is clinging. You don't need to find ignorance; it's said to be under all of them. Just notice, name, and return to the breath.

Avidya, ignorance, mistaking the passing for the lasting, the root of the five afflictions. Patanjali names it first, then I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life, all four growing in its field.
screen: `AVIDYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: five afflictions, one root: seeing wrongly. The yaksha's wonder is a good first place to look. That's the week.
